newsitem.title: FRANCE: Striking doctors out in force for Paris protest.
newsitem.headline: Striking doctors out in force for Paris protest.

text.p: Thousands of striking junior hospital doctors from across France demonstrated in Paris on Thursday, winning a meeting with cabinet ministers to discuss their protests at government plans to brake health spending.

Their 16-day-old strike has grown into a serious challenge to conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe's efforts to reduce France's welfare deficit as part of a drive to qualify for a single European currency in 1999.
The protesters waved banners, danced and chanted as they marched through the capital. Organisers put the crowd at 25,000, while police estimated it at 9,500.

As the protesters vowed to occupy Nation square through the night if the government refused to hear their complaints, Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot and Health Minister Herve Gaymard said they would meet their representatives on Friday.
Strikers from teaching hospitals as far away as Montpellier in the south and Rennes in the west marched in white coats daubed with anti-government slogans.
"The plan is a trap for morons," one coat read. "What about the sick?" another pleaded.
The junior practitioners are demanding the scrapping of fines on doctors if their region overshoots spending limits, and a renegotiation of agreements regulating their profession.
The plan challenges a traditional, virtually unlimited freedom of French doctors to consult and prescribe as they wish.
The strike has now spread to 22 of France's 26 teaching hospitals. Strikers are requisitioned to provide emergency care.
France spends a bigger slice of national wealth on health care than any industrialised country except the United States.
Public health spending is the biggest expense in the welfare system, expected to show a shortfall of 33 billion francs ($5.8 billion) this year.

Thousands of doctors gathered at the Place de la Bastille, a French revolution symbol, and marched to Place de la Nation, stopping at Pere Lachaise cemetery to "bury" the agreement in a mock ceremony with a coffin carried by medical students wearing green operating-theatre smocks.
The centre-right government has accused the strikers of promoting their sectional interests and vowed not to yield.

Juppe has sent 37 parliamentarians who trained as doctors to argue his case to the junior doctors, but the first ones were given a rough reception and one was prevented from leaving a teaching hospital in Bordeaux for several hours.

By Thursday the medical interns, who are supported by unions representing specialists in private practice, were joined by chief residents and some other hospital staff. But the action has not spread to the entire health profession and strikers acknowledge they face a tough fight.
"It's going to be hard," said Joanne, who came from Bordeaux. "But we're really motivated. We can win."
The largest medical union, MG France, representing general practitioners, opposes the strike and supports the Juppe plan.
The newspaper Le Monde said two big hospital doctors' unions and nurses opposed the strike, arguing that it ignored worsening conditions in hospitals hit by spending curbs.
Medical trade magazine Impact Medecin published an opinion survey on Thursday that found 81 percent of doctors questioned believed the strike was justified.
The survey of 330 French doctors in all disciplines between March 21 and 24 found that 70 percent of the respondents were worried about their future.
